title: PSI-9 Effect of replacing cottonseed hulls with a low-quality forage pellet on intake, digestion, and performance in growing Bos indicus steers.
content:
Abstract
Decreases in roughage supply and resultant increase in price has caused many beef producers to seek roughage alternatives, including lower-quality forages. One strategy to increase the utility of lower-quality forages is pelleting. Two experiments were conducted to evaluate the effect of replacing cottonseed hulls with a forage pellet on performance, digestibility, and ruminal fermentation in growing steers. In Exp. 1, 18 Brahman steers (initial BW = 246 ± 32 kg) were sorted according to initial BW and assigned to 1 of 7 pens. Within pen, steers were randomly assigned 1 of 2 dietary treatments: 1) 10% cottonseed hull (C10) and 2) 10% forage pellet (FP10). Steers were fed at 2.25% of BW as-fed split into two daily feedings. Steers were fed for 84 days, and bodyweight was recorded every 28. On d 85, all steers were transitioned to C10 for 4 days to account for differences in fill and reweighed on d 89. In Exp. 2, 5 ruminally cannulated Brahman steers (initial BW = 247 ± 13 kg) were used in a 2-treatment crossover design to quantify intake, digestion, and ruminal fermentation responses to a growing ration with a pelleted forage source. Dietary treatments were replicated from Exp. 1. Two 21-d periods were conducted with 15 days to adapt steers to treatments and 6 days to determine intake, digestion, and ruminal fermentation. In Exp. 1, no treatment effects (P > 0.10) were observed for final steer weight (331.5 kg), ADG (1.02 kg/d), as-fed intake (6.07 kg/d) and feed efficiency (0.170 kg gain/kg feed). In Exp. 2, there was no significant treatment effect on DM intake (4.77 kg/d; P = 0.87). However, OM intake was greater (P = 0.03) for C10 (4.40 kg/d) than FP10 (4.29 kg/d). In contrast, starch intake was greater (P = 0.05) in FP10 (0.50 kg/d) versus C10 (0.41 kg/d). There were no significant treatment effects (P ≥ 0.16) for digestion of DM, OM, NDF, and ADF. A tendency (P = 0.07) was observed for greater starch digestion in FP10 compared to C10 steers (99.6% and 98.4%, respectively). Accordingly, digestible starch intake was greater (P = 0.05) in FP10 than C10 (0.49 versus 0.41 kg/d, respectively). No treatment effects were observed for VFA concentration (P = 0.12), but a tendency was observed for pH to be lower (P = 0.09) with FP10 (6.10) than C10 (6.26) and for NH3 concentration to be greater (P = 0.06) for FP10 (8.40 mM) than C10 (5.17 mM). Similar performance, digestibility, and fermentation results with either cottonseed hulls or a forage pellet suggest that at equalized intakes, utilizing a pelleted, lower-quality forage source may be a suitable replacement for some commonly used roughages.
